pages.text: A complex number has two parts, a real part and a `j` part, so it needs two directions: the number line across for the real part, and a line of its own through 0, straight up, for the `j` part. This is the coordinate plane with its axes renamed: the [[complex plane]], also called an [[Argand diagram]].

pages.name: Read a dot
pages.task: Which number does this dot mark?
pages.why: Across first. The dot is 2 to the left of 0, so its real part is `−2`. Then up. It is 3 up, so its `j` part is 3. The dot marks `−2 + j3`.

pages.alt: The complex plane: real across, j up. 4 − j3 sits 4 across, 3 down. 6 + j0 sits 6 across, 0 up. 0 + j4 sits 0 across, 4 up. 4 minus j3: 4 across, 3 down. 6 plus j0: pure resistance. 0 plus j4: pure reactance.

pages.text: The two axes cut the plane into four quarters, and complex numbers sit in all of them. `4 − j3` is in the bottom right, 4 across and 3 down. With no `j` part, `6 + j0` lies on the real axis; with no real part, `0 + j4` lies on the `j` axis.

pages.name: Read an arrow
pages.task: Which number does this arrow show?
pages.why: The arrow ends 3 across, so the real part is 3, and 2 down, so the `j` part is `−2`. It shows `3 − j2`.

pages.alt: The plane, real across and j up. First arrow to 3 plus j1, second arrow to 1 plus j2. Laid tip to tail they finish at 4 plus j3. (3 plus j1) plus (1 plus j2): 4 plus j3. Real parts (across): 3 plus 1: 4. j parts (up): 1 plus 2: 3.

pages.why: Turn the second number half round. `−(1 − j3) = −1 + j3`. Then add. Real parts: `4 + (−1) = 3`. The `j` parts: `1 + 3 = 4`. The answer is `3 + j4`.

pages.name: (−2 + j5) + (2 − j5)
pages.why: Real parts: `−2 + 2 = 0`. The `j` parts: `5 + (−5) = 0`. The second arrow points exactly the opposite way to the first, so laid on its tip it leads straight back to 0. The sum is 0.

pages.name: w = (5 + j1) − (2 + j3)
pages.why: Turn the second number half round. `−(2 + j3) = −2 − j3`. Then real parts: `5 + (−2) = 3`, and the `j` parts: `1 + (−3) = −2`. So `w = 3 − j2`.
